navigation_summary: Read all 26 original u_*.py files plus INDEX.json (27 files total — the entire repo, since it's small and flat). There is no README, no runner/server/main file, no imports anywhere, and no tests. INDEX.json is the only structural document: it lists 26 "units," each with an id, a declared module grouping, a one-line purpose, an API signature string, an "effects" tag (store/net), and a "deps" list. File names are all u_<id>.py with zero folders. Critically, NONE of the .py files contain import statements, yet they reference names defined in other files (_tasks, _users, _projects, _tags, _comments dicts; functions like validate_title, hash_pw, genid, notify, format_date) with no NameError expected — meaning the real execution model is "concatenate/exec all units into one shared namespace," and INDEX.json's dep graph is presumably what some external loader (not present in this directory) uses to pick an order. I confirmed this by writing a throwaway harness that topologically sorts units by declared deps, execs them into one dict, and runs a scenario — it worked, confirming the flat-manifest execution model. The 'module' field in INDEX.json (auth, users, projects, tasks, tags, comments, notifications, search, pagination, dates, validate, ids) is purely descriptive metadata for humans/tools — it has no effect on Python file loading since there are no packages.
bugs_found: u_notify.py: local `encode()` reimplements base62 encoding with a 61-character CHARSET (missing 'Z'), duplicating and diverging from u_genid.py's correct 62-char encoder — produces different/colliding ref codes than genid() would for the same input (marked P1 in the code itself).
u_validate_email.py: validate_email() only checks the string is non-empty after stripping — accepts 'not-an-email', 'foo', etc. with no '@' or domain check (marked P2 in the code).

u_add_comment.py: local `_fmt()` reimplements date formatting as hours-since-epoch ('Nh'), inconsistent with the canonical u_format_date.py which formats as whole days ('day-N') — comments and everything else in the app display time in different, incompatible units (marked P3 in the code).

u_assign_task.py: assign_task(tid, uid, actor) accepts an `actor` parameter but never checks it against anything — any caller can reassign any task in any project to any user id, including nonexistent ones (marked P4 in the code).

u_paginate.py: paginate() computes `start = page * size` instead of `(page-1)*size` — for 1-indexed pages this skips the first `size` items entirely (page=1,size=10 returns items 10-19, dropping items 0-9) (marked P5 in the code).

u_hash_pw.py: hash_pw() sums ord(c) for all characters in the password — trivially collides for any anagram (e.g. 'ab' and 'ba' hash identically), and is not a real password hash (no salt, reversible via brute force on small sums).
u_make_token.py / u_check_token.py: tokens are just 't-<uid>' with no secret/signature — any client can forge a valid session token for any user id by guessing the format.

u_check_token.py: check_token() does int(tok[2:]) with no exception handling — a malformed token starting with 't-' but non-numeric (e.g. 't-abc') raises an unhandled ValueError instead of returning None.

u_create_task.py / u_complete_task.py / u_assign_task.py: none check that the given tid actually exists in _tasks before indexing into it — complete_task(999) and assign_task(999,...) raise raw KeyError instead of a clean error.
u_create_task.py: does not verify that `pid` refers to an existing project — a task can be created under a nonexistent project id.
u_create_project.py: does not verify that `owner` refers to an existing user id.
u_create_user.py: no uniqueness check on email — the same email can register multiple accounts, each with a different id.
u_add_tag.py: no dedup — the same tag string can be added to a task any number of times, and empty-string tags are accepted (no validate_nonempty call despite that utility existing).
u_add_comment.py: does not validate that `body` is non-empty, unlike create_task/create_project which both validate their text input.

u_uuid_like.py: contains a dead stub `from_ids_genid = None  # wired by layout` and the manifest declares uuid_like depends on genid, but the implementation never calls genid() at all — declared dependency doesn't match actual code, and the placeholder suggests an unfinished wiring.

u_notify.py: INDEX.json declares notify's effect as 'net' (implying it sends over a network), but the implementation only builds and returns a dict — no actual delivery/transport exists anywhere in the repo, so 'notification' is presently just an in-memory return value.

Systemic manifest gap: many units mutate or read module-level globals defined in a different unit's file (list_tasks/search_tasks/assign_task/complete_task all touch `_tasks`, which only u_create_task.py defines; list_projects touches `_projects` from u_create_project.py; get_user touches `_users` from u_create_user.py; list_tags touches `_tags` from u_add_tag.py; list_comments touches `_comments` from u_add_comment.py) — yet INDEX.json declares `deps: []` for every one of these. The manifest's dependency graph only tracks function-call deps, not shared-state deps, so trusting INDEX.json's deps list alone to pick a safe load order would break at runtime (e.g. loading list_tasks before create_task defines `_tasks` → NameError).
duplication_found: u_notify.py's encode() vs u_genid.py's genid() — same base62-encoding purpose, two divergent implementations (different alphabets), living in different files with no shared import.
u_add_comment.py's _fmt() vs u_format_date.py's format_date() — same 'format a timestamp' purpose, two divergent implementations (hours vs days) producing incompatible output formats across the app.

create_user, create_project, and create_task all independently implement the same 'next id = len(dict)+1' incrementing-id pattern inline rather than sharing one id-allocation helper (not currently buggy since nothing deletes rows, but it's the same logic copy-pasted three times and would break the moment a delete operation is added, since len() would then produce collisions).
missing_cases_found: No existence check on tid in complete_task/assign_task/set_due_date-adjacent flows before this change (set_due_date, which I added, does check tid exists — deliberately fixing that gap only for the new unit, not retrofitting the pre-existing ones, to keep the diff scoped to the feature).

No authorization: assign_task's `actor` param is accepted but unused (P4); by the same repo convention, my new set_due_date(tid, ts) also has no actor/permission check — flagged explicitly in a comment in u_set_due_date.py rather than silently added, since fixing authz repo-wide is out of scope for a feature patch.

No check that an assignee id actually corresponds to a real user anywhere (assign_task lets you assign to any int). This directly affects the new reminder feature, so check_due_reminders defensively calls get_user(uid) and skips tasks whose assignee doesn't resolve to a real user, rather than 'notifying' a nonexistent user.

No de-duplication for repeated reminder sends: a naive implementation re-run of a reminder scan would re-notify the same assignee every time it's called for as long as the task stays in the due window. I added a `reminded` flag on the task, cleared whenever set_due_date changes the due date, so each due date triggers exactly one reminder.

No distinction between 'due soon' and 'overdue' — an implementation that only checks `due - now <= window` without a lower bound of 0 would also fire for tasks that are already past due (arguably desirable for a different feature, but not what 'near its due date' asks for), so check_due_reminders requires `0 <= delta <= window_seconds`.
Off-by-one / boundary handling in paginate (P5, pre-existing) was left as-is since fixing it was not part of the requested feature, but is called out above as a bug worth fixing separately.

No validation that a due-date timestamp is non-negative before storing it — added a `ts < 0` check in set_due_date since nothing upstream validates timestamps at all (parse_date/format_date don't either).
feature_placement: Implemented as two new flat units, following the repo's own one-function-per-file convention exactly: u_set_due_date.py (set_due_date(tid, ts)->dict) under the existing 'tasks' module, and u_check_due_reminders.py (check_due_reminders(now_ts, window_seconds=86400)->list) under a new 'reminders' module (paralleling how 'notifications' already exists as its own module for u_notify.py). Both were registered as new entries in INDEX.json with purpose/api/effects/deps fields matching the existing entries' style. I also extended u_create_task.py's dict literal to include "due": None and "reminded": False fields (and gave create_task an optional due=None parameter) so every task has a consistent shape from creation, exactly mirroring how "assignee": None is already seeded there. check_due_reminders reuses format_date (for the message) and notify (for delivery) rather than inventing new formatting/notification logic, avoiding adding a third duplicate date-formatter to the two that already exist (format_date vs add_comment's _fmt). I verified the whole thing by writing a temporary harness (not part of the repo) that topologically sorts INDEX.json's units by declared deps, execs them into one shared namespace (matching how this manifest-only, import-free repo is clearly meant to be loaded), and ran a scenario proving: tasks with no due date are skipped, unassigned tasks are skipped, an assignee whose id doesn't resolve to a real user is skipped, overdue tasks are skipped, a task due soon gets exactly one notification, re-running the check does not double-notify, and changing the due date re-arms the reminder.
structure_helped_or_hurt: Mixed, net negative for a cold start. The flat, uniformly-named files (u_<verb>.py) plus INDEX.json's purpose/api summaries made initial orientation fast — I could read INDEX.json once and know the whole surface area (26 functions, their signatures, their intended module groupings) before opening a single implementation file, which is genuinely nice for a small repo. But the complete absence of imports across every file was disorienting the moment I opened individual units in isolation: u_list_tasks.py references `_tasks` with nothing in that file defining or importing it, and out of context that reads as a broken/incomplete file rather than an intentional cross-file global-namespace design. I only became confident about the actual execution model (concatenate-and-exec by manifest dep order) after reading essentially every file and noticing the pattern, then confirming it by building a throwaway loader — that's a lot of upfront cost for a 26-function app, and it would compound badly at 10x the size. The manifest's dep-list also actively misleads: it looks authoritative (it's the only 'structure' document in the repo) but silently omits every shared-mutable-state dependency, so trusting it at face value for load order would produce NameErrors. A newcomer who trusts INDEX.json's deps as complete would get burned. For adding the new feature specifically, the one-file-one-function convention was genuinely helpful — it made 'add two more files, add two more manifest entries' an obvious, low-risk move with an unambiguous place to put each new piece of logic, and there was never any doubt about which existing file to modify (u_create_task.py) versus where to add net-new files.

design: D_graph: a flat blobs/ directory of 26 (now 28) single-function Python files, each ~2-9 lines, plus one graph.json manifest that lists every blob as a node with a one-line `contract` signature and declares cross-blob dependencies as typed edges ("uses", and even a self-flagging "SHOULD_use_but_does_not"). There is no app.py, router, __init__.py, README, or tests anywhere. Blobs call each other and shared module-level dicts (_users, _projects, _tasks, _tags, _comments) by bare name with zero imports -- one file (uuid_like.py) has a leftover comment 'wired by layout' confirming some external step is expected to concatenate/exec the blobs into one shared namespace rather than the repo being directly runnable.
navigation_summary: Listed the whole directory first (find), which showed only blobs/*.py (26 files) and graph.json -- no entry point or docs. Read graph.json first as the only orientation document; it gave every function's contract and, unusually, already self-documented two of its own bugs via 'SHOULD_use_but_does_not' edges (notify should use genid but doesn't; add_comment should use format_date but doesn't). Then read all 25 remaining blob files in full since they're trivial (2-9 lines each) and graph.json's contracts don't show implementations -- that's where the P1-P5 bug comments and the shared-global wiring convention became visible. Built a throwaway exec-based harness (outside the repo, in-memory only) to actually load the blobs in dependency order and sanity-test the new feature end to end, since nothing in the repo is directly runnable.
bugs_found: P1 (notify.py): local encode() reimplements genid's base62 id encoder but with a 61-character alphabet (missing 'Z'), causing collisions; graph.json itself flags notify->genid as SHOULD_use_but_does_not.
P2 (validate_email.py): accepts any non-empty string as a valid email -- no '@' or domain check at all.

P3 (add_comment.py): private _fmt() reimplements date formatting differently (hours-since-epoch) from the canonical format_date.py (days-since-epoch); graph.json flags add_comment->format_date as SHOULD_use_but_does_not, so comment and task timestamps render in incompatible units.
P4 (assign_task.py): no authorization check that `actor` may assign tasks within the task's project -- the actor param is accepted but never used for anything.
P5 (paginate.py): off-by-one -- `start = page * size` instead of `(page-1)*size`, so calling with the natural first page (page=1) silently skips the first `size` items.
make_token/check_token: tokens are just "t-"+uid with no secret or signature and no expiry -- any caller can forge a valid token for any user id by string-building it.
hash_pw: 'hash' is sum(ord(c) for c in pw) -- massively collision-prone (e.g. 'ab' and 'ba' hash identically) and trivially invertible/guessable; not a real hash for auth.
uuid_like.py is dead, unused duplicate ID-generation logic (a second, never-wired id scheme alongside genid), with a leftover no-op line `from_ids_genid = None  # wired by layout`.
duplication_found: notify.py's encode() duplicates genid.py's base62 encoder with a broken alphabet (P1).
add_comment.py's _fmt() duplicates format_date.py's responsibility with a different, incompatible unit (P3).
uuid_like.py duplicates genid.py's entire 'generate an id' responsibility and is unused/dead.
missing_cases_found: create_task/create_project/assign_task never verify that pid/owner/uid reference an existing project/user -- e.g. create_task(9999, 'x') silently creates an orphaned task pointing at a nonexistent project, and assign_task(tid, 999, actor) assigns a nonexistent user with no error.
complete_task and assign_task index _tasks[tid] directly with no existence check -- an unknown tid raises an unhandled KeyError instead of a validation error.
No authorization/ownership checks anywhere that a caller may act on a given project's tasks (create_task, complete_task, add_comment, add_tag, and especially assign_task all skip this).
add_tag has no duplicate check -- the same tag can be appended to a task unboundedly many times.
No unassign path exists -- once assign_task sets an assignee there's no way to clear it back to None, and there's no delete for tasks/projects/users at all.
paginate off-by-one (P5, also listed under bugs).

For the new due-date reminder feature specifically: there is no 'already reminded' state, so calling check_due_reminders repeatedly while a task stays inside the due-soon window will re-notify every call -- documented in code as an intentional gap rather than silently hidden, since fixing it would require a new persistent field/flag beyond this feature's scope.
due_ts (new field) is completely unvalidated -- nothing stops a negative, non-integer, or already-past due date being set via create_task or set_due_date.
feature_placement: Added two new blobs following the repo's one-function-per-file convention: blobs/set_due_date.py (contract set_due_date(tid,due_ts)->dict, mutates the shared _tasks dict like complete_task/assign_task do) and blobs/check_due_reminders.py (contract check_due_reminders(now_ts,window_seconds)->list, scans _tasks for unfinished tasks whose due_ts falls within the window, skips tasks with no due date, no assignee, or an assignee id that doesn't resolve via get_user(), and calls the existing notify() for each qualifying task -- deliberately reusing notify()/get_user() rather than reimplementing them, to avoid repeating the P1/P3 duplicate-logic mistakes already present in this codebase). Also extended create_task.py with an optional due_ts=None third parameter (backward compatible) so a due date can be set at creation time, not only after. Registered both new nodes plus the extended create_task contract in graph.json, and added explicit 'uses' edges from check_due_reminders to notify and get_user, matching the manifest's existing pattern of declaring cross-blob dependencies as graph data rather than Python imports. Verified the feature by writing a throwaway exec-harness (not committed to the repo) that wires all blobs in dependency order and confirmed reminders fire only for tasks that are due-soon, unfinished, assigned, and have a real assignee -- correctly skipping a far-future task, an unassigned task, a task with a ghost (nonexistent) assignee, and a completed task.

navigation_summary: Structure: a flat REGISTRY.json manifest listing every "capability" (id, owning package, one-line signature) plus one package per concern under packages/<name>/impl.py (auth, comments, dates, ids, notifications, pagination, projects, search, tags, tasks, users, validate). There is no app.py, server, __init__.py, requirements file, or test suite anywhere in the directory -- I read every file that exists (11 impl.py files + REGISTRY.json, 12 total) before editing anything. The defining and disorienting trait: impl.py files call each other's functions and even each other's module-level globals (e.g. packages/search/impl.py reads `_tasks`, a dict only ever defined in packages/tasks/impl.py; packages/tasks/impl.py calls `validate_title` with no import; packages/users/impl.py calls `validate_email`, `hash_pw`, `genid` all bare) with zero import statements anywhere in the codebase. None of these modules can run standalone via normal Python semantics -- they only work if something outside this directory execs/merges all impl.py files into one shared namespace, and REGISTRY.json documents the id->package mapping but contains no loader code itself; no such loader exists inside this directory. I confirmed the wiring convention (and that my new feature actually works) by writing a throwaway harness that exec'd all 12 files into one dict in a dependency order I inferred by hand, then called through it end to end. The registry's flat capability table was genuinely useful for orientation -- a one-screen index of every public function and its home package, better than grepping cold. But the missing composition root was a real cost: I could not import or run anything the normal way, nothing in the directory states the real load order, and I had to reverse-engineer the "shared namespace" convention from bare-name references rather than trusting an import graph -- a fragile way to keep a codebase together, and one an editor/IDE "go to definition" would not follow at all.
bugs_found: packages/notifications/impl.py: local encode() reimplements base62 id-encoding with a 61-character CHARSET (missing 'Z') instead of reusing packages/ids.genid's 62-character alphabet -- same algorithm, different alphabet size, so the same seq number maps to a different string in each package (e.g. any n where n%61 vs n%62 diverges); duplicated AND wrong (pre-existing, marked P1 in comments).
packages/validate/impl.py validate_email(): accepts any non-empty string, no '@' or domain check at all, so create_user('not-an-email', pw) succeeds (pre-existing, marked P2).

packages/comments/impl.py _fmt(): reimplements timestamp formatting locally as hours-since-epoch ('Nh'), completely different unit and output format from packages/dates.format_date's days-since-epoch ('day-N') -- same kind of data (a unix ts) formatted two incompatible ways depending on which package touches it (pre-existing, marked P3).
packages/tasks/impl.py assign_task(): takes an `actor` argument but never checks it -- any actor can reassign any task in any project, no authorization check at all (pre-existing, marked P4).

packages/pagination/impl.py paginate(): off-by-one, uses `page*size` instead of `(page-1)*size`; with page=1 (the natural first page) it skips the first `size` items entirely, and page=0 returns what callers would expect page=1 to return (pre-existing, marked P5).

packages/auth/impl.py hash_pw(): 'hashing' is just sum(ord(c) for c in pw) -- trivially collides (e.g. 'ab' and 'ba' hash identically, as do any two anagrams, or 'ac'/'bb'), so verify_pw() will accept wrong passwords whose character-sum happens to match. Not a hash function in any real sense.

packages/auth/impl.py make_token()/check_token(): token is literally 't-' + uid with no signature, secret, or expiry -- any client can forge a valid token for any user id by string-concatenating 't-<uid>'; check_token() will happily accept it.

packages/tasks/impl.py complete_task() and assign_task(): both index `_tasks[tid]` directly with no existence check, so an unknown tid raises a raw uncaught KeyError instead of a validated error -- inconsistent with create_task/create_project/create_user, which all raise ValueError on bad input.

packages/tasks/impl.py create_task() and packages/projects/impl.py create_project(): neither validates that the referenced pid/owner actually exists, so tasks can be created under nonexistent projects and projects under nonexistent owners -- no referential integrity anywhere in the data model.

packages/tasks/impl.py assign_task(): also never checks that `uid` refers to an existing user, so a task can be assigned to a nonexistent user id (which would then also silently swallow due-date reminders, since notify() is never told the uid doesn't exist).
packages/users/impl.py create_user(): no duplicate-email check -- the same email can register N different user ids with N different passwords.
packages/users/impl.py create_user(): pw is hashed but never validated (not run through validate_nonempty or any length/strength check), so an empty-string password is accepted.
packages/tags/impl.py add_tag(): no dedup and no case normalization -- adding the same tag (or 'Bug' vs 'bug') twice produces duplicate entries in list_tags().

packages/search/impl.py search_tasks(q): calls `q.lower()` with no None/type check -- passing q=None raises AttributeError instead of a validated error; also matches only on title, silently ignoring tags/comments a caller might expect to be searched.

create_task/create_project/create_user all mint ids via `len(collection) + 1` -- with no delete operation currently exposed this happens not to collide today, but it's a latent id-reuse bug the moment any delete capability is added (two different records could get the same id after a deletion), and it's duplicated across three packages instead of shared via packages/ids.
packages/pagination/impl.py paginate(): no validation on page/size -- size<=0 or page<0 is not rejected and produces confusing/empty/negative-index slice behavior instead of a clear error.

packages/ids/impl.py: leftover dead line `from_ids_genid = None  # wired by layout` -- an unused variable whose name and comment gesture at some external wiring mechanism that isn't actually implemented anywhere in this directory (see design note above about missing composition root).
duplication_found: Base62/id-style encoders exist independently in packages/ids/impl.py (genid, 62-char alphabet) and packages/notifications/impl.py (encode, 61-char alphabet) -- same algorithm shape, different and incompatible alphabets (see P1 above).

Timestamp formatting exists independently in packages/dates/impl.py (format_date, days-since-epoch) and packages/comments/impl.py (_fmt, hours-since-epoch) -- same input type, two different and incompatible human-readable outputs (see P3 above).
'Mint next id as len(dict)+1' logic is copy-pasted identically across packages/tasks, packages/projects, and packages/users instead of being one shared capability (e.g. reusing packages/ids).
missing_cases_found: No authorization check in assign_task on the `actor` parameter it already accepts (P4) -- I did not add one since the task scope was the reminder feature, but it directly borders the new set_due_date/check_due_reminders capabilities I added, which likewise take no actor and enforce no permission that the caller may set a due date or trigger reminders on a task outside their project.

No existence validation for tid in complete_task/assign_task (raw KeyError) -- I kept set_due_date consistent with that existing (bad) pattern for tid, documented inline, rather than silently diverging; flagging it here since it's a real gap either way.

No check that a project/user id referenced by a task actually exists (create_task doesn't validate pid, assign_task doesn't validate uid) -- means check_due_reminders could in principle be asked to notify a uid that was never created; notify() itself does no existence check either.

No de-duplication guard existed anywhere before my change for 'notify the same person about the same thing twice' -- I added a `reminded` flag specifically because without one, calling check_due_reminders repeatedly (e.g. on every poll of a scheduler) would re-notify the same assignee every single tick until the due date passed.

No upper bound / sanity check on ts values passed to set_due_date beyond type and positivity -- a caller can set a due_date arbitrarily far in the past or future with no validation against 'now' at set-time (only checked later when scanning for reminders).
feature_placement: Implemented as two pieces, following the repo's existing package-per-capability convention: (1) added `set_due_date(tid, ts)` to packages/tasks/impl.py (task data owner, alongside assign_task/complete_task, mirroring how the existing state-mutation setters live next to task storage) and initialized `due_date`/`reminded` fields on task creation; (2) added a brand-new packages/reminders/impl.py with `check_due_reminders(now_ts, threshold_seconds)`, registered as a new capability in REGISTRY.json. I put the scanning/notification logic in its own package rather than folding it into packages/tasks or packages/notifications because it is a distinct capability that reads task state (via the bare `_tasks` global, the same cross-package convention packages/search already uses to reach into packages/tasks) and calls the existing `notify()` capability -- exactly the shape of every other package in this repo (one focused capability, wired to others by name, registered once in REGISTRY.json). I verified it works by exec'ing all impl.py files into one namespace (the only way to actually run this codebase) and confirmed: a task with an assignee and a near due date gets exactly one notification, a second scan does not re-notify, changing the due date re-arms the reminder, and tasks with no assignee or already done are correctly skipped.

navigation_summary: Repo is a "fractal manifest" layout: a root INDEX.json lists 12 child module directories (ids, validate, dates, auth, users, projects, tasks, tags, comments, notifications, search, pagination), each with its own INDEX.json (a manifest of `id`/`api` signatures) plus an impl.py. Crucially, NONE of the impl.py files import anything from each other — e.g. users/impl.py calls validate_email, hash_pw, genid with zero imports; ids/impl.py has a literal comment "from_ids_genid = None  # wired by layout". This told me the actual wiring (concatenating/exec'ing all impl.py files into one shared namespace, in the order the root INDEX.json lists them) lives in a harness outside this directory that I was told to ignore/not assume. I verified my hypothesis was correct by writing a throwaway smoke-test script that reads INDEX.json's children list, exec's each impl.py into one dict, and calls the resulting functions — it worked with zero import errors, confirming the "flat shared namespace, ordered by manifest" model. I read the root manifest, then every one of the 12 leaf INDEX.json+impl.py pairs (24 files) — actually I batched most reads together since each file is tiny (3-20 lines), so total distinct files opened was 14 read calls covering all ~22 existing files plus the 2 I wrote (reminders/INDEX.json, reminders/impl.py).
bugs_found: auth.hash_pw uses sum(ord(c) for c in pw) as a 'hash' - trivially collision-prone (any anagram of a password hashes identically) and not a real cryptographic hash at all - severe auth weakness.
auth.make_token/check_token: token is literally 't-'+uid with no secret/signature, so any client can forge a valid token for any user by constructing the string themselves - full auth bypass.

notifications.encode is a second, independently-written base62-style encoder (61-char alphabet, missing 'Z') duplicating ids.genid (62-char, full alphabet) for the same conceptual purpose (turning a sequence number into a short ref) - same input produces two different, inconsistent 'ids' depending on which module encoded it (pre-flagged in-file as P1).
validate.validate_email accepts any non-empty string - 'not an email' passes validation with no @ or domain check (pre-flagged in-file as P2).

comments._fmt reimplements timestamp formatting independently from dates.format_date, using hours-since-epoch ('12h') instead of the canonical days-since-epoch ('day-12') format used everywhere else - comment timestamps and task due-date timestamps are displayed in silently incompatible units (pre-flagged in-file as P3).
tasks.assign_task accepts an `actor` argument but never checks it - any actor can reassign any task in any project with no membership/ownership check (pre-flagged in-file as P4).

pagination.paginate computes start = page*size instead of (page-1)*size, so page=1 (the natural first page) skips the first `size` items entirely, and there is no page/size validation (e.g. size<=0 returns garbage) (pre-flagged in-file as P5).

tasks.complete_task and tasks.assign_task do zero existence check on tid - both raise a raw KeyError straight to the caller for an invalid tid, which I also found true of the get/set surface I extended (documented via my set_due_date's own existence check, which the two pre-existing functions lack).

search.search_tasks reaches into the tasks module's private _tasks dict directly and searches across ALL projects/tasks regardless of the caller's project - no pid scoping and no auth check, so it's a cross-project data leak, and it will crash with AttributeError/TypeError if q is None.
duplication_found: notifications.encode duplicates ids.genid (base62 sequence encoder) with a different, buggy alphabet - two implementations of the same concept with diverging outputs.
comments._fmt duplicates dates.format_date (timestamp -> human string) with a different, incompatible unit (hours vs days) - same concept, two diverging implementations.
missing_cases_found: No 'due date' field existed on tasks at all before this change - had to add it (create_task(due=None) + new set_due_date) since the reminder feature has nothing to key off otherwise.

No dedup/anti-spam for reminders - a naive implementation would re-notify the same assignee every single scan for as long as a task stays in the due-soon window; I added a _notified[tid]->due_ts cache in reminders/impl.py so a reminder fires once per (task, due_ts) pair, and added clear_reminder_state(tid) so a due-date change can re-arm it.

No existence check in the pre-existing complete_task/assign_task (tid not validated) - raw KeyError leaks to callers; I did add the check in my new set_due_date but did not go back and fix the two pre-existing functions since that's scope creep beyond the reminder feature (flagged instead).

No handling for 'overdue' (due date already passed) as distinct from 'due soon' - my is_due_soon only covers 0<=due-now<=threshold; a task that's already overdue never gets a reminder under this implementation. Documented as a deliberate scope limit rather than silently redefining 'due soon' to include the past - a real system would likely want a separate overdue-escalation path.

No authorization check on who may call scan_due_reminders for a given pid (consistent with the rest of the codebase's total absence of project-membership checks) - flagged, not fixed, since fixing auth pervasively is out of scope for this feature.

Unassigned tasks and completed tasks are both explicitly guarded against in check_task_reminder (skip, don't error) - these are the two most obvious missing-case traps for a 'notify the assignee' feature and I made sure both are covered with tests.
feature_placement: Implemented as a new leaf module reminders/ (INDEX.json + impl.py), sibling to tasks/ and notifications/, and registered it in the root INDEX.json's children list. Also extended tasks/impl.py's create_task to accept an optional due=None field and added a new set_due_date(tid,due) unit (mirrored in tasks/INDEX.json). The reminders module follows the exact same convention as every other module in this layout: zero import statements, calling notify() (from notifications/), format_date() (from dates/), and list_tasks() (from tasks/) as bare names, on the assumption - which I verified by writing a throwaway harness that execs every child impl.py from the root manifest's children list into one shared dict, in manifest order, and ran it - that some out-of-directory harness (correctly out of scope per the task rules) concatenates/execs all impl.py files into one shared namespace at runtime. I did not wire tasks.set_due_date to call reminders.clear_reminder_state automatically, since that would make the base tasks/ module depend on the higher-level reminders/ module, inverting the layering the manifest tree implies; instead clear_reminder_state is exposed for whatever caller changes a due date to invoke explicitly.
structure_helped_or_hurt: Mostly helped, with one real friction point. Helped: the one-concern-per-directory split made orientation fast - 14 small reads (most files are 3-20 lines) were enough to see the entire app's surface, and each INDEX.json's `units` list is a genuinely useful table of contents that let me skim signatures before reading bodies. It also made the pre-planted bugs easy to spot since each is isolated to one tiny file with a comment pointing at it. Hurt: the total absence of import statements across every single file (confirmed real, not an oversight, via the 'wired by layout' comment in ids/impl.py) means you cannot open any one file and know where its free variables come from, or run/test a single module in isolation - I had to reconstruct the implied 'exec everything from the root manifest in listed order into one namespace' harness myself with a throwaway script just to smoke-test that my new module's calls to notify/format_date/list_tasks would actually resolve at runtime, since nothing in the visible repo proves that wiring works. That's a meaningful tax relative to a normal package with explicit imports, and it's also risky: adding reminders/ to the root INDEX.json children list in the wrong position, or before notifications/dates/tasks are exec'd, would silently break it depending on how the (out-of-scope, unseen) harness actually orders things - I placed it after notifications/ and dates/ defensively but couldn't fully verify the real harness's ordering rules from inside this directory alone.

design: G_contract_bus: each domain gets a contracts/X.py file (one-line "# contract: fn(args)->ret # description" comments per function — a spec-only header, zero executable code) paired with an impl/X.py file (the actual implementation). There are exactly 12 domains (auth, comments, dates, ids, notifications, pagination, projects, search, tags, tasks, users, validate), 24 files total, 147 lines total. No package __init__.py, no main.py/app.py/router, no tests, no README — nothing ties the pieces together at runtime.
navigation_summary: Read every file in the repo (all 12 contracts/*.py + all 12 impl/*.py, 147 lines combined) — the tree is small enough that a full read was faster than trying to search-and-guess. The contracts/ directory read like an index/table-of-contents (one-line signatures with intent), which was genuinely helpful for orientation — I knew the full public surface area in under a minute. But it actively misled me about wiring: contracts/tasks.py implies assign_task, complete_task etc. all just work, while impl/tasks.py calls validate_title(title) with no import of it anywhere in the file or package. I initially assumed a 'bus' module somewhere merged all impl namespaces together (matching the design name), searched for main.py/app.py/bus.py/__init__.py, and found none — so I ran the impl functions directly to check, and confirmed by execution (not just reading) that impl/tasks.create_task, impl/projects.create_project, impl/users.create_user, and impl/search.search_tasks all raise NameError today. The 'contract' files are pure documentation with no enforcement (no ABC, no runtime check, nothing importing them) — they describe an interface nothing binds to. Net effect: the pairing convention *helped* me locate 'where does X live' instantly, but the missing wiring layer implied by 'bus' in the design name is simply absent, so the structure oversold a level of integration the code doesn't have. I had to add explicit imports in my own new code to make it actually runnate, rather than following the (broken) house style of bare cross-module calls.
feature_placement: Added the feature entirely inside the existing tasks domain: contracts/tasks.py gained two new one-line contract entries (set_due_date(tid,ts)->dict and check_due_reminders(now_ts,window_seconds=86400)->list), and create_task's contract line was updated to accept an optional due_ts. impl/tasks.py got matching code: each task dict now carries due_ts and a reminded flag; set_due_date updates the due date and re-arms the reminder; check_due_reminders scans tasks in id order and, for each task that is not done, has an assignee, has a due_ts, and has not already been reminded, checks whether 0 <= due_ts - now_ts <= window_seconds and if so calls the existing notifications.notify(uid, msg, seq) and marks the task reminded so it isn't re-notified on the next scan. This is the correct location because tasks.py already owns the task lifecycle (create/list/complete/assign) and the contracts/impl split makes 'which file owns which verbs' unambiguous — a due-date reminder is a task-lifecycle concern that happens to call out to the notifications domain, exactly like assign_task calls out to nothing but plausibly should call notify too (it currently doesn't — see missing_cases). I explicitly imported notify and format_date from impl.notifications / impl.dates at the top of impl/tasks.py rather than following the codebase's existing convention of bare unimported cross-module calls, because that existing convention is actually broken (see bugs_found) and I wanted the new feature to be runnable, not just stylistically consistent with broken code. I verified it end-to-end by executing it: a task due in 1h got exactly one notification, a re-run did not double-notify, an overdue task and an unassigned task were correctly skipped, and calling set_due_date re-armed the reminder for a follow-up notification.
bugs_found: FUNDAMENTAL/unlabeled: the implied wiring layer ('bus') does not exist anywhere in the repo. impl/tasks.py calls validate_title(), impl/projects.py calls validate_nonempty(), impl/users.py calls validate_email()/hash_pw()/genid(), and impl/search.py references _tasks — none of these names are imported or defined in those files. I proved by execution (not inspection) that impl.tasks.create_task(1,'x'), impl.users.create_user('a@b.com','pw'), impl.projects.create_project(1,'p'), and impl.search.search_tasks('a') all raise NameError today. Nothing in the repo currently runs.

P1 (impl/notifications.py): local `encode()` reimplements base62 with a 61-character CHARSET (missing 'Z'), so it mods by 61 instead of 62 — different seq values collide on the same ref code (verified: this duplicates ids.genid's logic but is subtly wrong, and is a separate near-duplicate of the bug below).

impl/ids.py genid(n) has no handling for negative n: the while loop condition `n > 0` is false immediately, so genid(-5) silently returns '' instead of raising or erroring. Same latent bug likely in notifications.encode.
P2 (impl/validate.py): validate_email only checks non-empty-after-strip — no '@' or domain check, so 'not-an-email' passes and create_user('not-an-email','pw') succeeds.

P3 (impl/comments.py): _fmt() reimplements date formatting differently and incompatibly from dates.format_date (hours-since-epoch string vs. dates.py's 'day-N' format) — same conceptual value formatted two incompatible ways depending on which module renders it.
P4 (impl/tasks.py): assign_task(tid, uid, actor) takes an `actor` parameter but never checks it — any caller can reassign any task in any project to any user id with no authorization check at all.

P5 (impl/pagination.py): paginate() computes `start = page * size` instead of `(page - 1) * size` — page=1 skips the first `size` items entirely (off-by-one), and page=0 would return items starting at index 0 (works by accident) but there's no validation that page >= 1.

impl/auth.py hash_pw sums character ordinals — this is a checksum, not a hash: any anagram of a password hashes identically (verified: hash_pw('ab') == hash_pw('ba') == 'h$195'), so verify_pw accepts wrong passwords that happen to share a character multiset.
impl/auth.py make_token(uid) just returns 't-' + str(uid) — tokens are trivially guessable/forgeable from a user id alone; there is no secret, expiry, or signature.
impl/auth.py check_token('t-') (a token missing the numeric suffix) raises an uncaught ValueError from int('') instead of returning None as its own contract promises for malformed input.
duplication_found: impl/notifications.py's encode() is a near-duplicate of impl/ids.py's genid() (same base62-encoding algorithm) but with a different, broken 61-char alphabet — two implementations of 'the same idea' that now disagree.

impl/comments.py's _fmt() duplicates the responsibility of impl/dates.py's format_date() (turning a unix timestamp into a display string) but produces a different, incompatible format — same concept, two divergent implementations in different domains.

impl/ids.py has a dead/vestigial line `from_ids_genid = None  # wired by layout` — its own comment explicitly admits it expected an external 'layout'/bus mechanism to wire it up, and nothing ever does; it's unused dead code that documents the missing-wiring problem in its own right.
missing_cases_found: No authorization/ownership check anywhere that a task belongs to the project the caller thinks it does, or that a user is a member of a project before being assigned/creating tasks in it (create_project/create_task never check the acting user has any relationship to the owner/project).

search_tasks(q) searches across ALL tasks globally regardless of project or requester — no scoping, so any user can discover titles of tasks in projects they don't own (authorization/data-leak gap), and it does not handle q='' or q=None (would either match everything or crash on .lower()).
create_user never checks email uniqueness — two accounts can register the same email address.
assign_task never validates that uid refers to an existing user (get_user(uid) is never called), so a task can be 'assigned' to a nonexistent user id.

No delete/remove/unassign operations exist anywhere in the domain (tasks, projects, comments, tags) — only create/list/(complete|assign) — so mistakes (wrong tag, wrong assignee, wrong comment) are permanent.

add_comment/add_tag never validate tid exists (a comment or tag can be attached to a nonexistent task id with no error) and add_tag never checks for duplicate tags (the same tag can be added to a task N times).
add_comment never validates body is non-empty even though validate_nonempty exists right there in the codebase for exactly this purpose.

For my new due-date reminder feature specifically: there's no validation that due_ts is in the future when set via create_task/set_due_date (a caller can silently set a due date in the past); there's no re-notification/escalation policy for tasks that go overdue after being missed (once 'reminded' is set true, an overdue task never gets a second, more urgent notice); and window_seconds isn't validated to be >= 0 in check_due_reminders.
paginate() never validates page >= 1 or size > 0, compounding the P5 off-by-one — page=0 or negative size produce silently-wrong slices rather than errors.
structure_helped_or_hurt: Mixed, leaning hurt. The contracts/ directory as a one-line-per-function index was a genuine win for orientation — I could see the entire public surface area (12 domains, ~30 functions) in under a minute without reading a single line of implementation, and it told me unambiguously which file owns which verb (so placing set_due_date/check_due_reminders in tasks.py was a non-decision). But the split actively hurt in the more important way: the contracts describe a working system ('assign_task(tid,uid,actor)->dict') and imply some 'bus' wires implementations to each other, but no such wiring exists anywhere in the repo — the impl files call functions from sibling domains with zero imports, so most of the pre-existing code (create_task, create_user, create_project, search_tasks) throws NameError the instant it's actually executed. I only caught this by running the code, not by reading it; a reader trusting the contracts/impl pairing at face value would believe the app works. So the structure optimized for 'looks organized, easy to find things' at the cost of 'is actually runnable' — I had to deviate from the codebase's own convention (bare unimported cross-calls) and add real imports in my new code just to make the feature I wrote functional.

navigation_summary: I read every one of the 26 files in the directory because the layout offered no shortcut: there is no README, no entry point, no import statements anywhere, and no test suite. Each file is exactly one function (occasionally with a private module-level dict acting as its "table"), prefixed with a `# effects: [...]` comment, and EFFECTS.json is a manifest listing every unit's id and declared effects (store/net/none). Every cross-file call is a bare-name reference into what must be a shared namespace assembled by something outside this directory — uuid_like.py even has a comment "from_ids_genid = None  # wired by layout" confirming this. Since nothing in the directory documents the actual wiring mechanism or order, I inferred it from EFFECTS.json's array order and verified by writing a throwaway harness that concatenates and execs every file in that order into one dict, then exercised both the existing functions and my new one against it (including a reassignment/dedup scenario) to confirm real behavior, not just code reading. The one-function-per-file convention forced opening literally everything up front — cheap per file but many round trips — since no file hints at what else exists; once the "flat namespace, effects-tagged, one function per file" convention clicked, adding to it was mechanical and low-risk.
bugs_found: notify.py (pre-marked P1 in source): local base62 encode() uses a 61-character CHARSET (typo drops 'Z') vs genid.py's correct 62-char alphabet — a near-duplicate encoder that also silently produces colliding notification refs for larger sequence numbers.
validate_email.py (pre-marked P2): accepts any non-empty string — no '@' or domain check at all — so create_user() happily stores garbage emails.

add_comment.py (pre-marked P3): its private _fmt(ts) reimplements time formatting as hours-since-epoch ('Nh'), diverging from the canonical format_date.py (days-since-epoch, 'day-N'). Two different date-formatting conventions coexist in the same app.
assign_task.py (pre-marked P4): actor parameter is accepted but never checked — no verification that actor has permission over the task's project, so any caller can reassign any task to anyone.
paginate.py (pre-marked P5): off-by-one — start = page * size instead of (page-1) * size, so page=1 (if pages are meant to be 1-indexed) skips the first `size` items entirely.

hash_pw.py: password hash is sum(ord(c) for c in pw) — trivially collides (any anagram of a password, e.g. 'ab' and 'ba', hashes identically), and is not a real cryptographic hash at all; verify_pw inherits this weakness completely.

make_token.py/check_token.py: auth tokens are just 't-' + uid with no signature/secret — completely forgeable (anyone can compute another user's token by guessing their id), and check_token does int(tok[2:]) with no try/except, so a malformed token like 't-abc' raises an uncaught ValueError instead of returning None/failing cleanly.
check_token.py never confirms the decoded uid actually exists (no get_user check) — a token for a deleted or never-created uid still 'validates'.

create_task.py / create_project.py / create_user.py all mint ids as len(dict)+1 — duplicated id-generation logic across three files (instead of reusing genid.py/uuid_like.py which already exist for exactly this), and it's fragile: if any delete function is ever added, len()+1 will start reissuing already-used ids.
create_task.py never validates that pid refers to an existing project — orphaned tasks under nonexistent projects are silently allowed.
create_project.py never validates that owner refers to an existing user.
assign_task.py never validates that tid exists (raises an uncaught KeyError for a bad id) or that uid refers to a real user — you can assign a task to a nonexistent user id.
complete_task.py has the same unguarded _tasks[tid] pattern — completing a nonexistent task raises an uncaught KeyError instead of a clean error.
create_user.py never checks email uniqueness — two users can register with the identical email.

search_tasks.py has no project/owner scoping — it searches every task in the entire store regardless of who is asking, i.e. anyone can enumerate task titles across projects they don't own (authorization/data-leak gap), and paginate.py exists but is never wired into list_tasks/list_projects/search_tasks despite being built for exactly that purpose.
add_tag.py never checks tid exists and never dedups — the same tag can be appended to a task an unbounded number of times.

uuid_like.py is dead code: the module-level `from_ids_genid = None` stub is never read or set by anything, and uuid_like() itself is never called by any other unit in the repo — leftover/unused scaffolding.

format_date.py/parse_date.py: format_date floors to whole days (ts // 86400), so parse_date(format_date(ts)) != ts in general — a lossy, non-invertible round trip that looks invertible from the naming.
duplication_found: notify.py's encode() vs genid.py's genid(): same base62-style id-encoding algorithm reimplemented twice, one copy with a typo'd 61-char alphabet.
add_comment.py's private _fmt(ts) vs format_date.py's format_date(ts): two independent, inconsistent date-formatting implementations for the same concept.

create_task.py, create_project.py, create_user.py: identical 'id = len(_dict) + 1' id-minting logic copy-pasted three times instead of centralized (and duplicating what genid.py/uuid_like.py already do).
validate_nonempty.py vs validate_title.py: near-identical non-empty/length string validators kept as two separate units.
missing_cases_found: No existence check for pid when creating a task, or for owner when creating a project (referential integrity is entirely unenforced).
No authorization check anywhere: assign_task ignores its actor param, complete_task/add_comment/add_tag take no caller identity at all, so any code path can mutate or read any task/project/comment.
No email-uniqueness validation in create_user.

No due-date-in-the-past validation beyond non-negativity in the create_task change I made — a due date already in the past is accepted (arguably correct for backfilled data, but worth a product decision).
check_token has no handling for malformed tokens (uncaught exception) and doesn't confirm the resulting uid still exists.
paginate is disconnected from every list/search function that would need it, so there's effectively no working pagination in the app despite the utility existing.

For my own feature: without care, reassigning a task after its first reminder would silently never notify the new assignee — I fixed this by keying the dedup set on (task_id, assignee) rather than task_id alone, and verified it with a live test (first assignee notified once, then reassignment to a second user triggers a fresh notification to them).
feature_placement: Added a new file check_due_reminders.py (one function per file, matching the repo's universal convention) tagged `# effects: ['store', 'net']` since it reads the shared _tasks store and calls the net-effect notify(). It takes `now` as an explicit parameter rather than calling a clock internally, matching the existing convention of passing timestamps in (e.g. add_comment(tid, ts, body)) so the effect surface stays exactly as declared. It references _tasks, get_user, format_date, and notify as bare globals — the same 'flat shared namespace, no imports' pattern every other file uses (confirmed by writing a harness that concatenates all files in EFFECTS.json order and exec's them together, then running the new function against real data). I also added an optional `due` field to create_task.py (with basic type/non-negativity validation) since tasks previously had no due-date field at all, and registered the new unit in EFFECTS.json with its effects, exactly as every existing unit is registered.
structure_helped_or_hurt: Mixed, leaning 'hurt for orientation, helped for insertion.' It hurt discovery: 26 single-function files with zero imports and zero entry point meant I could not run anything or trust my mental model until I built my own concatenation harness — nothing in the directory documents how the pieces are actually wired together at runtime, so I had to reverse-engineer the convention from a single comment ('wired by layout') plus EFFECTS.json's ordering, and I could easily have gotten that wrong. It helped insertion, though: once the convention was clear, adding a new capability was completely mechanical and low-risk — one new file, one EFFECTS.json entry, one small additive edit to an existing file — with no risk of breaking unrelated code since every unit is already isolated by construction. The effects tags were genuinely useful documentation (I could tell at a glance which functions touch storage vs. network before reading their bodies).

navigation_summary: The repo is a flat chunks/ directory (26 one-function .py files) plus a README that says outright "No manifest. Each file starts with an @card block (purpose/api/tags/deps) meant for semantic retrieval." There is no app.py, router, package __init__.py, or any actual `import` statement anywhere in the directory. Since it's small (26 files) I just read every file rather than trying to search selectively -- with no manifest/entry point there was nothing to navigate FROM, so a targeted search would have missed the real story, which is architectural: every chunk assumes a set of shared globals (_tasks, _users, _projects, _comments, _tags) and calls other chunks' functions by bare name (e.g. assign_task.py calls _tasks[tid] without ever defining or importing _tasks; complete_task.py, list_tasks.py, search_tasks.py do the same). The `deps:` field in each @card is pure retrieval metadata, not executable wiring -- these files cannot run as independent modules; they only work if something (absent from this directory) execs/concatenates them all into one namespace. I verified this by writing a throwaway harness that exec'd all chunks into a shared dict and called the new feature end-to-end, which is the only way to actually validate behavior here. The lack of a manifest fought me in the sense that I had to infer the execution model myself (nothing states it), but once inferred, the one-function-per-file + @card convention was easy to extend consistently.
bugs_found: notify.py P1: encode() uses a 61-character CHARSET (missing 'Z') while doing `% 61`/`// 61` base-62-style math -- this is a broken/duplicate reimplementation of genid.py's correct 62-char encoder and will produce colliding ref codes for different seq values.
validate_email.py P2: validate_email only checks the string is non-empty after stripping -- no '@' or domain check, so create_user accepts any garbage as an email.

add_comment.py P3: the local _fmt(ts) helper formats timestamps as '<hours>h' (ts//3600), which is a completely different unit/format from the canonical format_date.py ('day-<days>', ts//86400) -- comment timestamps and task/due-date timestamps are displayed inconsistently across the app.

assign_task.py P4: assign_task(tid, uid, actor) takes an `actor` argument but never checks that actor has any permission to assign within the task's project -- any caller can reassign any task to anyone.
paginate.py P5: `start = page * size` instead of `(page - 1) * size` -- off-by-one for a 1-indexed page API (page=1 skips the first `size` items).

make_token.py / check_token.py: tokens are just 't-' + uid with no signature/secret -- check_token will accept a hand-constructed string like 't-1' as a valid session for user 1. This is a forgeable-auth bug, not just a weak-crypto one.
hash_pw.py: 'hashing' is sum(ord(c) for c in pw) -- trivially collides for any anagram (e.g. 'ab' and 'ba' hash identically), and verify_pw inherits this weakness.
create_user.py: no duplicate-email check -- two users can register with the same email address.

complete_task.py and assign_task.py: no existence check on `tid` -- `_tasks[tid]` raises an uncaught KeyError for an unknown id, while add_comment.py and add_tag.py silently accept comments/tags for a nonexistent tid via setdefault(). The two families of 'mutate a task' functions disagree on how they fail for a bad id.
check_token.py: `int(tok[2:])` throws an uncaught ValueError for malformed tokens like 't-' or 't-abc' instead of returning None -- the declared return type is `int|None` but it can also just crash.
search_tasks.py: `q.lower()` will raise AttributeError if q is None; no guard for a missing/None query.

create_task.py / create_project.py / create_user.py: IDs are generated via `len(dict) + 1`, which is fragile (would produce duplicate/reused IDs if any deletion path is ever added) and duplicates the purpose of the already-present genid.py/uuid_like.py id utilities, which sit unused for this purpose (uuid_like.py isn't called by any create_* function at all).

uuid_like.py contains `from_ids_genid = None  # wired by layout` -- a vestigial stub implying an import that never happens anywhere in the repo; dead code left over from an assumed wiring layer that doesn't exist in this directory.

Systemic: none of the 26 chunk files contain a single `import` statement, yet they reference each other's functions and shared globals (_tasks, _users, _projects, _comments, _tags) freely. As shipped, no two of these files can be run together without an external harness that execs them into one namespace -- there is no manifest, __init__.py, or app entrypoint anywhere in the directory to do that. This is the most significant structural issue in the repo.
duplication_found: notify.py's encode() duplicates genid.py's base62 encoder, but reimplements it locally with a different (buggy, 61-char) alphabet instead of importing/reusing genid.
add_comment.py's _fmt() duplicates the purpose of dates/format_date.py but reimplements it with a different, inconsistent time unit (hours vs days).

create_task.py, create_project.py, and create_user.py each hand-roll the same `id = len(store) + 1` id-generation pattern instead of sharing one id-allocation helper (genid.py and uuid_like.py already exist for this purpose but are bypassed for primary keys).

list_tasks.py, list_projects.py, search_tasks.py, list_comments.py, and list_tags.py all reimplement the same 'filter a dict's values and return a list' shape by hand rather than sharing a helper, and none of them call the existing paginate.py, so any endpoint returning a large collection has no consistent pagination behavior.
missing_cases_found: No authorization check anywhere that the actor performing an action (assign_task, complete_task, set_due_date, add_comment, add_tag) actually owns or is a member of the task's project -- assign_task even accepts an `actor` param and ignores it entirely.

No existence validation for tid/pid/uid across almost every mutating function (assign_task, complete_task, set_due_date, add_comment, add_tag, create_task's pid, create_project's owner) -- callers can silently create orphaned data or hit an uncaught KeyError.
No duplicate-email check on user creation.
No password strength/non-empty check in create_user (hash_pw('') succeeds silently).
check_token has no handling for malformed tokens (crashes instead of returning None) and no expiry/revocation concept at all.
paginate has no validation for page < 1 or size <= 0 (would silently return [] or misbehave rather than erroring clearly), on top of the off-by-one bug.

For the due-date reminder feature itself: no handling of already-overdue tasks (only 'approaching due date within a window' is covered -- a task that blows past its due date without ever being completed gets exactly one reminder near the deadline and then silence forever, no escalation). This is called out inline in check_due_reminders.py's docstring/comment as a deliberate scope choice worth revisiting.

No timezone/clock-source handling anywhere in the date utilities (format_date/parse_date/set_due_date/check_due_reminders) -- all timestamps are bare unix ints with no stated timezone convention, so 'due soon' is only as correct as whatever now_ts the caller supplies.
feature_placement: Added chunks/set_due_date.py (api: set_due_date(tid, due_ts)) mirroring the existing assign_task.py pattern -- due date is set via a dedicated setter chunk rather than folded into create_task, matching how assignee is set via assign_task rather than at creation. Added chunks/check_due_reminders.py (api: check_due_reminders(now_ts, window_seconds=86400)) which scans the shared _tasks store and calls the existing notify.py chunk for every not-done, assigned task whose due_ts falls within the window and hasn't been reminded yet (dedup via a new 'reminded' flag on the task dict). Also edited chunks/create_task.py to add 'due_ts': None and 'reminded': False to the task dict literal, since those are now part of the task schema (same file that already defines the _tasks store and the task shape). This keeps the one-function-per-file / @card convention intact and reuses the existing notify() chunk rather than inventing a new notification path, which is the placement the repo's established (if unwired) conventions implied.
structure_helped_or_hurt: Net: hurt more than it helped. The one-function-per-file + @card metadata convention was clear and easy to extend once understood (mirroring assign_task.py's shape for set_due_date.py was straightforward), and it's genuinely good for RAG retrieval of individual functions. But the complete absence of a manifest, entrypoint, or any `import` statement meant I had no way to verify the feature actually works without building my own exec-based test harness to simulate whatever real wiring layer is missing from this directory -- I had to reverse-engineer the execution model (shared-globals-via-exec) purely from behavioral evidence (undefined names referenced across files) rather than from anything the repo states. For a 26-file repo reading everything was cheap, but the design would not scale, and it left me unable to confirm with any confidence that my new files will actually be loaded/wired the same way the existing ones apparently are outside this directory.

navigation_summary: Directory contains exactly two files: README.md (one line: "Single-file app. Jump via `# region:<name>` anchors listed in the TOC header.") and app.py (a flat 200-line single-file service layer with no framework/routes — just plain functions backed by module-level dicts as in-memory stores). app.py opens with a hand-maintained "TABLE OF CONTENTS" comment block listing every function's region name, signature, and one-line purpose, in the same order the regions appear in the file, each function then wrapped in `# region:name ... # endregion:name` markers. I read the whole file once (it's short enough), which was enough to understand every entity (users, projects, tasks, tags, comments, notify, search, paginate) and every store (_users, _projects, _tasks, _tags, _comments) without needing to grep or open anything else. No tests, no config, no second module existed to check.
bugs_found: P1 (already flagged in source, but worse than the comment states): notify's region redefines the module-level `CHARSET` variable (61 chars, missing 'Z') to a different value than genid's region (62 chars) — since both are the same global name in one module, the second definition silently overwrites the first at import time. This doesn't just make encode() collision-prone as the inline comment claims; it also breaks genid() itself. Verified: `genid(61)` raises `IndexError: string index out of range` because genid indexes with `n % 62` into a string that is actually only 61 chars long after the overwrite, and other genid() outputs are silently wrong/colliding too. This directly affects create_user, which calls genid(uid) for every new user's 'code' field.
P2 (flagged in source): validate_email(s) accepts any non-empty string — no '@' or domain check at all, so create_user('not-an-email', pw) succeeds.

P3 (flagged in source): add_comment's local `_fmt(ts)` implements timestamp formatting as hours-since-epoch, completely independently from and inconsistent with the canonical `format_date(ts)` (days-since-epoch) used everywhere else — same operation duplicated with different, incompatible units.
P4 (flagged in source): assign_task(tid, uid, actor) takes an `actor` parameter but never checks that actor has any permission over the task/project — any actor can reassign any task to any uid.

P5 (flagged in source): paginate(items, page, size) does `start = page * size` instead of `(page-1) * size` — page 1 skips the first `size` items entirely (there is no valid 'page 0' to get them back), an off-by-one that makes the first page unreachable.

hash_pw(pw) is `sum(ord(c) for c in pw)` — a checksum, not a hash. Any anagram of a password produces the identical hash (e.g. 'ab' and 'ba' collide), so verify_pw would accept a wrong password with the same character multiset. No salt, trivially invertible in spirit.
make_token/check_token: session tokens are literally 't-<uid>' with no secret/signature/expiry — any client can forge a valid session for any user id by constructing the string themselves.

check_token(tok): if a token starts with 't-' but has a non-numeric suffix (e.g. 't-abc'), `int(tok[2:])` raises an uncaught ValueError instead of returning None, contradicting its own documented `->int|None` signature.
duplication_found: encode()/CHARSET in the notify region duplicates genid()/CHARSET in the genid region — same base-N encoding logic reimplemented with a broken alphabet and a colliding global name (source-flagged as P1).

_fmt() in the add_comment region duplicates format_date() in the format_date region — same conceptual operation ('format a unix ts for display'), reimplemented with different, incompatible units (hours vs days) (source-flagged as P3).
missing_cases_found: create_task(pid, title) never validates that pid refers to an existing project — a task can be created against a nonexistent project id with no error.
create_project(owner, name) never validates that owner refers to an existing user.

complete_task, assign_task, add_tag, add_comment, list_tags, list_comments, and my new set_due_date all do direct dict lookups (_tasks[tid]) with no existence check, so a bad tid raises a raw KeyError instead of a clean domain error.
assign_task doesn't check that uid refers to an existing user — a task can be assigned to a nonexistent user id, which would also make it silently un-notifiable by the reminder feature.

search_tasks(q) searches across ALL tasks globally with no project/owner scoping and no authorization check — any caller can search any other user's task titles; also raises AttributeError if q is None (no type guard).
paginate has no validation that page >= 1 or size > 0, beyond the off-by-one itself; size<=0 or negative page produce silently odd/empty slices rather than an error.

No authorization/session layer ties any query function (list_projects(owner), list_tasks(pid), etc.) back to a resolved session user via check_token — every function trusts whatever id the caller passes in; assign_task's unchecked `actor` param is the only place this gap is even acknowledged in-code, and only via a comment, not a fix.

Notification delivery had no memory at all before this change: notify() just returned a dict and stored nothing, so nothing could list, audit, or deduplicate what had been sent — which is exactly the gap a due-date reminder needs to not spam the same task repeatedly. I extended notify() to persist into a new _notifications log and added list_notifications(uid) as a companion query, matching every other store's list_* convention in the file.
feature_placement: Implemented entirely inside app.py, following the file's own conventions rather than adding new files or layers (there are none to hook into — no routes, no ORM, no service/module split). Specifics: (1) added `due` and `due_reminded` fields to the task dict in create_task, defaulting to None/False so existing behavior for tasks without a due date is unchanged; (2) added `validate_due_date(ts)` alongside the other validate_* functions; (3) added a dedicated `set_due_date(tid, due_ts, actor)` mutator placed right after assign_task, matching the file's one-function-per-mutation style (rather than overloading create_task with an extra due-date argument) — it re-arms `due_reminded` to False whenever the due date changes, so a pushed-out or pulled-in deadline is re-evaluated; (4) extended `notify()` to persist every sent notification into a new module-level `_notifications` log (it previously persisted nothing at all) and added `list_notifications(uid)` as its list_* companion, consistent with every other store in the file; (5) added the feature's entry point, `check_due_reminders(now, window_seconds=86400)`, placed directly after notify/list_notifications since it's their consumer — it scans _tasks, skips done tasks, tasks with no due date, tasks already reminded, and tasks with no assignee (documented as a deliberate no-op edge case, not an error), and calls notify() for tasks overdue or within the window, using format_date() for the message text rather than re-implementing date formatting a third time. (6) Updated the TOC header with new region entries for validate_due_date, set_due_date, list_notifications, and check_due_reminders in the same order they appear in the file, preserving the TOC's role as an accurate index. Verified via a manual smoke script: fires for near-due and overdue assigned tasks, is idempotent on repeated calls, correctly holds off on unassigned tasks until assigned, re-arms when due date changes, and rejects a negative due date.
structure_helped_or_hurt: Helped, clearly and mostly for one reason: the hand-maintained TOC-with-region-anchors pattern is unusually good for both human and agent navigation at this file size. I could read the whole 200-line file once and immediately know every function's signature, purpose, and location without grepping, and I never had to search for 'where does X live' — the TOC answered it up front, and the region markers made insertion points unambiguous (new validator goes next to other validate_* regions, new mutator goes next to assign_task, new query goes next to notify). There is no framework/route layer to reconcile a feature with, which removed a whole category of 'where does this plug in' ambiguity that a typical web-app layout would have. The one thing working against this structure is not something I hit but something worth flagging: the TOC is free-text and manually kept in sync by convention only (nothing enforces it), and it will not scale gracefully as this pattern is pushed toward a real production-sized file — it works cleanly here because 200-290 lines is small enough to hold in one read. Also, several existing bugs (P1's shared-global CHARSET collision, P3's duplicated date formatter) were only findable by literally reading every region rather than by pattern-matching the TOC descriptions, since the TOC's one-line descriptions don't surface implementation defects — the flat/no-encapsulation layout is exactly what let two same-named globals silently collide across regions in the first place.

design: A_flat_manifest: every function is its own file `u_<name>.py` with NO imports; shared mutable stores (`_tasks`, `_users`, `_projects`, `_tags`, `_comments`) are module-level globals that only resolve because a loader concatenates all units into one namespace. `INDEX.json` is the authoritative registry (id, module, api, effects, deps) — it is the map the layout hands you in place of a package tree.
model: Domain: users, projects, tasks (belong to a project, have assignee + done flag), tags, comments, notifications, plus auth (token/hash), dates (day-granular `day-N` <-> unix ts), search, pagination. Tasks had NO due-date field before this change. State lives in per-file dicts keyed by an incrementing `len(dict)+1` counter. Auth is toy-grade: `make_token(uid)='t-'+uid`, `check_token` just parses the suffix.
navigation_summary: INDEX.json gave a fast, honest orientation (modules, per-unit api, effects, deps) and pointed me straight at `notify`/`format_date` for reuse and at `create_task` as the tasks store owner. But because there are zero imports, the manifest is the ONLY thing tying units together — 'go to definition' is dead, and to understand data flow for tasks I had to open every unit that mentions `_tasks` (create/list/complete/assign/search) individually since the shared global is invisible from any single file. Discovery via manifest was cheap; verifying runtime behavior meant hand-simulating the loader by concatenating units, because no file is independently runnable.

Date formatting: `dates.format_date` (day-based) vs `u_add_comment.py::_fmt` (hour-based) — two divergent formatters (P3).
ID-counter pattern `len(_store)+1` copy-pasted across create_task, create_user, create_project.
`uuid_like`/`genid`/`create_user.code` are three overlapping id-encoding schemes; `u_uuid_like.py` even has a dead `from_ids_genid = None  # wired by layout` stub that is never used.
